title: Tensor Networks for Materials Simulation and Quantum Chemistry
authors: Saeed S. Jahromi, Augustine Kshetrimayum, Roman Rausch, Sukhbinder Singh, Roman Orus
abstract: Predicting the properties of correlated materials and molecules often requires a many-body description that goes beyond single-particle and mean-field approximations. Tensor networks address this challenge by exploiting the entanglement structure of quantum states to construct compact, systematically improvable representations. Although developed largely for idealized model Hamiltonians, these methods are increasingly being integrated into material-specific calculations. This Perspective introduces their underlying principles and examines how network geometry, bond-dimension truncation, and approximate contraction determine the accuracy and computational reach of these approaches. We survey applications across regimes of increasing complexity, ranging from ground-state properties of quantum magnets and itinerant-fermion systems to excitation spectra, nonequilibrium dynamics, finite-temperature and open systems, and molecular electronic structure. We then examine four routes connecting these methods to real materials, including experimentally constrained models, downfolded Hamiltonians, dynamical mean-field theory with tensor network impurity solvers, and quantum embedding. Throughout, we evaluate the maturity of existing capabilities and their principal limitations, synthesizing this assessment into a practical method-selection guide. We argue that reliable materials predictions require quantifying uncertainties introduced at each stage, from constructing material-specific Hamiltonians to extracting experimentally accessible observables. Finally, we identify the algorithmic advances and reproducible computational practices needed to establish tensor networks as a routine tool for predictive materials science and quantum chemistry.
summary: This perspective review details how tensor networks offer a powerful, systematic method to simulate strongly correlated quantum materials and molecules. It surveys various network types and computational routes, emphasizing that accurate predictions require careful quantification of approximation errors at every step. The work aims to establish TNs as a routine, reliable tool for predictive quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The core challenge is predicting the properties of correlated materials and molecules, which necessitates descriptions beyond simple single-particle or mean-field approximations.
main_result: Tensor networks provide a systematically improvable, nonperturbative framework to tackle these complex many-body problems, moving the field toward routine predictive materials science.
method: The paper surveys the use of various tensor network representations (MPS, PEPS, MERA) to encode quantum states and Hamiltonians, allowing for controlled approximations based on entanglement structure.
model_or_system: The scope covers a wide range of systems, including quantum magnets, itinerant-fermion systems, molecular electronic structure, and strongly correlated oxides (like cuprates).
key_observables: Ground-state properties, excitation spectra, non-equilibrium dynamics, finite-temperature observables, and correlation functions.
important_parameters: The bond dimension ($\chi$) is the critical parameter controlling accuracy, alongside the entanglement structure and the choice of network geometry.
main_assumptions: Reliable predictions require rigorously quantifying uncertainties introduced at every stage, from Hamiltonian construction to the final observable extraction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general structure of TNs, showing how they replace exponential amplitudes with tensors connected by bond indices, and map out the four main computational routes connecting TNs to real materials.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the principles of TNs, surveys their applications across increasing complexity (from simple models to open systems), examines four specific computational routes to real materials, and concludes with a practical guide on method selection and necessary algorithmic advances.
why_interesting: The systematic and controlled nature of TN approximations, particularly their ability to handle entanglement structure, provides a powerful, non-perturbative tool for simulating complex quantum dynamics relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of tensor networks. (a) The dN amplitudes of a many-body wavefunction are replaced by a chain of N small tensors connected by bond indices of dimension χ; the bond dimension controls both the retained entanglement and the cost. (b) An important basis for compression is the area law obeyed by many ground states of local Hamiltonians: the entanglement entropy of a region A scales with its boundary ∂A rather than its volume. (c)–(f) The network geometry follows the entanglement structure: matrix product states (MPS) for chains and ordered orbitals, tree tensor network states (TTNS) for branched correlations, projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) for two-dimensional...

Figure 2: The operations underlying every tensor network calculation. (a) An expectation value is the full contraction of the state, the operator, and the conjugate state. (b) Truncation by singular value decomposition keeps the χ largest Schmidt coefficients; the discarded weight ε measures the norm lost at that cut and helps assess convergence. (c) To update or measure one tensor, the rest of the network is summarized in its environment, which is exact for chains and trees but must be approximated for PEPS. Figure 3: A map of tensor network applications to materials. The horizontal axis orders the Hamiltonian from an idealized spin model to a material-specific ab initio description; the vertical axis orders the observable from a ground-state phase to nonequilibrium and open-system response. Each marker is a representative calculation discussed in Secs. 3 and 4, coloured by the maturity of the capability it exemplifies. The historical development of the field runs along the diagonal from model ground states toward material-specific spectra and dynamics.

Figure 4: Routes from a real material to an experimentally testable tensor network prediction. Structure, composition, and sample conditions feed one of four material-specific constructions: a model Hamilto- nian constrained by experiment, a downfolded Hamiltonian from electronic structure, a self-consistent impurity problem from dynamical mean-field theory, or an embedded fragment with an algebraic bath. A tensor network solver returns the state or correlation function from which observables are extracted and compared with experiment. Uncertainty enters at every interface (orange), and disagreement with experiment should feed back to the model or the input rather than only to the solver.
